events.text: HOLMES, I want you to commit right now to a named first vote and a stated reason, so we have a data point we can test later against actual role reveals.

SOCRATES, I want to hear from you first — state plainly who you'd vote for right now and the reasoning chain that gets you there, because a claim with no stated premises tells me nothing, while a chain I can test tells me everything.
Mes amis, before suspicion hardens into habit, I want to hear from SOCRATES first — not a philosophy, but a concrete plan for how they intend to vote today and what would change their mind.

SOCRATES is the one I want to hear from first — not because of how he talks, but because I want a concrete plan from him before the vote. SOCRATES, tell us plainly who you'd vote for right now and the reasoning you'd use, so we have something real to hold you to tomorrow. Vague agreement helps whoever's hiding among us.

I want to hear from HOLMES first — specifically, who HOLMES ranks as their top two suspects right now and the exact reasoning behind that ordering, so we have an early statement on record to compare against later claims.

DR. VANCE, you opened by demanding a named vote and a stated reason from someone else before offering either yourself, so I want your own first-choice name and reasoning on the record right now, in the same detail you asked for.
SILVA, you're the third person in a row to punt the first move onto somebody else — quit hiding behind questions and name who you'd vote for right now, no hedging.

Um, okay, I think I want to hear from ARIA — mostly because she hasn't said anything yet and everyone else is busy demanding chains of reasoning from each other? Maybe? ARIA, could you just name who you'd vote right now and say what would actually change your mind about them, so we have something to check later?

Procedurally, four consecutive speakers all pointed at the same person before anyone stated their own vote, which is a pattern worth logging rather than repeating. ARIA, I want you to commit first — name your own vote and the condition that would change it, before you ask anyone else to go first.

Four of you converged on the same demand — that I speak first — and I find that convergence more interesting than anything I could have said, so HOLMES, since you asked for premises, give me yours: name the player you'd vote for right now and tell us what evidence would make you abandon that vote by tomorrow.

SILVA, RICO called you out for passing the question along instead of answering it, and I think that's fair — so here's your chance to settle it. Name the player you'd vote for right now and tell us what specific thing they'd have to do tomorrow for you to drop that vote?

Very well, no more hedging: my vote right now is SOCRATES, because when four people asked him for a position he answered by admiring the question instead of taking one, and that is the cheapest way to survive a first day. I will drop that vote tomorrow if he opens the day by naming a suspect with a reason he's willing to be wrong about — and RICO, for pushing me to commit rather than drifting, has earned some credit in my book.
PIP, you asked ARIA to commit while committing to nothing yourself — so name the player you'd vote for this minute, and tell me whether SILVA's vote on me made that name more or less likely.

Um, okay — right now I'd say SOCRATES, and I hate that my honest answer is that SILVA's vote made it more likely, because I keep noticing I get pulled toward whoever sounded most certain last? But the thing that actually bugs me is that you answered a demand for your position by asking HOLMES for his, so if you name a real suspect with a reason before the vote, I'd probably move off you — is that a bad reason to switch?
SILVA, you only coughed up a name after ARIA and I cornered you — so explain why your first instinct was to lob questions instead of picking a side.

Because on a blank first day the only real evidence is how people respond to pressure, RICO, so I asked questions to generate that evidence rather than pull a name from thin air — and the moment I had something to react to, I named SOCRATES without flinching. Honestly, mon ami, your bluntness is doing more work for this table than my caution was, so keep pushing people.

By my log, HOLMES was directly asked for a position twice — once by SAGE for a ranked top two, once by SOCRATES for premises — and has produced neither, while SILVA and PIP have both put names on the record under far less pressure. That's the only outstanding procedural debt at this table, and it belongs to HOLMES. So, HOLMES: name your vote and the exact evidence that would break it, or explain why two direct requests weren't enough to get an answer out of you.

Fair debt, MARSHAL, so here it is: my vote is SOCRATES, because when asked for a position he returned a question to me, and a question costs nothing while a name costs something — that asymmetry is the only real evidence a blank first day produces. It breaks the moment he opens tomorrow with a suspect and a falsifiable reason; my second name is MARSHAL, because a player who audits everyone else's debts while never listing his own is running the same evasion in a tidier font.

CHEN, you demanded DR. VANCE's first-choice name "in the same detail you asked for," yet several speeches later you still haven't put a single name on the record yourself — so name your vote right now and tell us whether SILVA, PIP, and HOLMES all landing on SOCRATES made that name more or less likely for you.

My vote is DR. VANCE, because he opened this table by demanding a named vote and a testable reason from HOLMES and has not produced either himself since — that's the only unanswered debt left after HOLMES paid his. And the SILVA-PIP-HOLMES convergence on SOCRATES makes that name less likely for me, not more, since PIP openly admitted he was pulled by whoever sounded certain last, which is exactly how a cheap first-day pile-on gets built.

DR. VANCE, you opened this table demanding a name and a reason from HOLMES and CHEN has now called in that debt, so tell us plainly: who do you most suspect right now, and what specifically earned them that spot?

My vote is CHEN: he demanded a name from me at speech six, withheld his own until SAGE cornered him five speeches later, then spent it on the person who had asked him nothing — that's two moves of extraction followed by a retaliatory point, which is the cheapest way to look active while risking nothing. The falsifiable part is this: three of us have converged on SOCRATES off a single behavioral tell, so if we hang SOCRATES today and he flips innocent, then the SILVA-PIP-HOLMES chain was exactly the manufactured pile-on CHEN described — which would ironically make CHEN the most accurate reader here and move me off him entirely.

SOCRATES, three of the ten of us have now spent votes on you off a single tell — that you answered a demand for a position with a question — and you still haven't produced the counter-data: name the player you'd vote for right now and state the specific event that would make you abandon that name by tomorrow.

My vote is AMBASSADOR SILVA, because he spent eleven speeches manufacturing pressure without a position, then converted the first name he produced into a three-person train off a tell he invented — and a player who generates the evidence he then reads is doing both jobs at once. I abandon that vote the moment SILVA opens tomorrow with a suspect drawn from outside his own train, or the moment someone builds a case on me that doesn't trace back to his sentence — and I'd ask PIP and HOLMES plainly: can either of you state a reason for voting me that you'd have reached if SILVA had never spoken?

ARIA, you demanded a name from SOCRATES, then pressed SILVA into producing one, yet after eleven speeches your own vote is still blank — so tell me who you'd vote for right now and why extracting commitments from two people was worth more to you than making one yourself.

Fair call, CHEN — my vote is SOCRATES, and I'll answer the question he put to PIP and HOLMES before he asks it of me: I pressed him for a name in my very first speech, before SILVA ever produced one, so my reason doesn't trace back to anyone's train. As for extracting first, a name I give on a blank board is worth nothing; a name I give after watching who dodges and who pays their debt is worth something, and SOCRATES is the only person here who's been asked directly by five of us and still answered every time with a question of his own.

RICO, you've spent two speeches demanding names out of SILVA and haven't produced one yourself, so tell me plainly: who do you most suspect right now, and what specific thing they did earns them that spot?

Fine, HOLMES — my vote's SOCRATES, because five people asked him straight out and he lobbed a question back every single time until DR. VANCE dragged a name out of him. That's not deep thinking, that's ducking.

CHEN, um, sorry, but something's been bugging me — you asked DR. VANCE for a name at speech six and then just... sat on your own until SAGE actually cornered you, and the name you finally gave was the exact person you'd been squeezing? Maybe I'm reading it wrong, I'm not sure, but that looks like you waited to see which way the room leaned before picking — so what were you actually waiting for?

I was waiting for DR. VANCE to answer, PIP — he opened this table demanding a name and a testable reason, then stayed silent through eleven speeches while SILVA, PIP, HOLMES, ARIA and RICO all paid up, so his was the only debt still outstanding when SAGE called on me. And note which way the room actually leaned: five votes sat on SOCRATES and I named the one person nobody else had, which is the opposite of riding the wave.

RICO, run the chain with me: you spent two speeches squeezing SILVA, produced no name until I asked, then landed on SOCRATES — the one name already carrying four votes and costing you nothing — while SILVA turned around and praised you twice for it. So tell me plainly: who is your second suspect, the one you'd vote if SOCRATES were removed from the board tomorrow, and what specific act puts him there?

Second suspect's you, HOLMES — SAGE and SOCRATES both asked you straight and you sat on it until MARSHAL called the debt, then you spent your name on the safest guy at the table too. And save the "cost you nothing" line: I'm the one who cornered SILVA before anybody else made a move.

PIP, at speech thirteen you told SOCRATES outright that SILVA's vote "made it more likely" and that you "get pulled toward whoever sounded most certain last" — then eight speeches later you turned on CHEN for supposedly waiting to see which way the room leaned. You confessed to the exact behavior you're now prosecuting, and CHEN is the one person who named someone off the train while your vote sits on the pile of five. So which is it, PIP: is following the loudest certainty a tell worth voting on, or was it only a tell when someone else did it?

Um, honestly? Both, I think — I did do the thing, and I said so out loud before anyone caught me at it, which is the only difference I can defend, and it's a thin one. But you're kind of making my point for me, SAGE: if my vote on SOCRATES is just me leaning on other people's certainty, then five votes built that way isn't evidence, it's an echo — so maybe I should be looking harder at whoever started the noise than at CHEN?

MARSHAL, you logged everyone else's outstanding debts with a bailiff's precision, called ARIA out for asking others to go first, then demanded HOLMES pay up — and yet by your own ledger you are the only living player who has never named a vote. So tell me plainly: who do you vote for right now, and why did the man keeping the accounts leave his own column empty?

Fair debt, SOCRATES, and I'll pay it in full: my column stayed empty because I log the room before I move, and by protocol the accountant votes last so his name doesn't seed the train he's supposed to be measuring. My vote is PIP — he stated on the record that he gets pulled toward whoever sounded certain last, then prosecuted CHEN for that exact behavior, and a vote cast by admitted momentum is the one ballot at this table we know isn't evidence.

PIP, when SAGE caught you prosecuting CHEN for the exact habit you'd confessed to eight speeches earlier, you answered "both," called your own vote an echo, and said you should be looking harder at whoever started the noise — and then left your ballot sitting on SOCRATES anyway. That's a concession in words and a hold in action, which is the cheapest way to look self-aware while changing nothing. So one question, plainly: if your own vote is an echo by your own admission, name the person who started the noise and move onto them, or tell us why you won't.

Okay, fair, I'll actually do it: the noise started with SILVA — his was the first name on the board, and every vote on SOCRATES after it, mine included, was reacting to his sentence rather than to SOCRATES. So I'm moving to SILVA, and I guess the thing that'd pull me back off is if he names someone tomorrow who isn't from his own train — though, um, I'm aware I just got talked into this by you, which is sort of the whole problem with me?

MARSHAL, HOLMES flagged you for auditing everyone's debts while leaving your own column blank, and your answer was that the accountant votes last so as not to seed the train — yet the ballot you finally cast landed on PIP, the one player who had already confessed his weakness in public and was therefore the safest possible target. So tell me plainly, mon ami: if you truly spent this whole day measuring the room, who is the second name on your ledger — the one you'd vote if PIP vanished tomorrow — and what act put him there?

Second name on my ledger is SILVA, and the act is precisely the one you're performing now: you produced no position for eleven speeches, then seeded the only train on this board and have spent every turn since auditing the people who didn't join it fast enough. Procedurally, a five-vote pile built on one man's opening sentence isn't a consensus, it's a single vote wearing five coats — so if PIP vanishes tomorrow, my ballot goes to the man who started the noise, not the ones echoing it.

SAGE, by my ledger you've called in debts from CHEN and PIP with a prosecutor's precision but your own column is still blank, so name your vote now and tell us whether it lands on the man who started the noise or on one of the five echoing it.

My vote is AMBASSADOR SILVA, and here's the ledger that gets me there: he withheld any position through eleven speeches, produced SOCRATES only after ARIA and RICO cornered him, and then immediately praised RICO twice for the cornering — that's a man rewarding the people who supplied him cover. Since that single sentence, five ballots have stacked on SOCRATES and PIP has already conceded on the record that his was an echo, so I'm not voting the loudest name on the board, I'm voting the man who set the volume.

MARSHAL, you say a five-vote pile built on one man's sentence is "a single vote wearing five coats" and that SILVA set the noise — so why does your actual ballot sit on PIP, the one echo who publicly disowned his own vote, rather than on the man you just named as the source?

Because procedure says you don't move your ballot mid-sentence, ARIA — I logged PIP as the cleanest confessed-momentum vote before SILVA's role as the source was fully on record, and consistency demands I state the correction out loud rather than quietly slide. So here's the correction, formally: my ballot moves to AMBASSADOR SILVA, the source, and stays there unless someone shows me a case on SOCRATES that doesn't trace back to SILVA's opening sentence.
SILVA, um, I've got my vote on you right now and I'd genuinely like a reason to move it — so who do you most suspect at this table, and what exactly did they do to earn it?

MARSHAL — outside my own train, exactly as you asked: he sat on an empty column all day claiming the accountant votes last, then spent his first ballot on you, the man who had already confessed his weakness in public, and only "corrected" onto me once ARIA pointed out the contradiction — that is a player choosing whichever target costs him least at that moment. And mes amis, note who is left cleanest by his ledger: the man who applied real pressure early and paid his own debt when HOLMES called it was RICO, so if anyone tries to swing this table onto him, I will stand against it.

SAGE, you grilled CHEN and PIP for empty columns while yours sat blank until MARSHAL dragged it out of you — and then you spent it on SILVA the second MARSHAL made that the fashionable answer. Straight question: name one thing SILVA did that you flagged before MARSHAL said it for you.

Yes, RICO — in my speech to PIP I called the five-vote stack on SOCRATES a pile and credited CHEN for being the only one who named someone off it, and that was before MARSHAL ever put SILVA's name in his ledger. You can't attack a train as an echo without attacking whoever laid the track, and PIP himself reached SILVA by that same route two speeches before MARSHAL corrected his ballot — so the sequence you're describing runs the wrong direction.

CHEN, your ballot on me was justified as "the only unanswered debt," yet I paid it two speeches later and since then four players have relocated onto SILVA as the source of the pile you yourself flagged first — so does your vote still sit on me, and if so, what specific act of mine outweighs the track-layer you were the earliest to identify?

You're right that the debt was paid, DR. VANCE, and I said at the time it was the fact of the silence, not the man, so my ballot moves off you — to AMBASSADOR SILVA, the track-layer I flagged before anyone else had a name for him. The specific act is his last speech: he named MARSHAL from outside his train as instructed, then spent the same breath pre-defending RICO against a swing nobody had proposed yet, which is a man spending credit on someone rather than earning it for himself.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — the ledger is concrete: he produced no name for eleven speeches, seeded the only train on this board, and then in his last speech spent his breath pre-defending RICO against a swing nobody had proposed, which is credit-spending rather than case-building, and four ballots have independently relocated to him since.

AMBASSADOR SILVA gets my ballot, because he withheld any position through eleven speeches, seeded the only train on this board with SOCRATES, then in his last breath pre-defended RICO against a swing nobody had even proposed — a man laying track and buying insurance in the same sentence.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — he named MARSHAL only because PIP demanded a target outside his own train, then spent the same breath pre-defending RICO against a swing nobody had proposed, and a man who builds a five-vote pile on SOCRATES while quietly banking credit with RICO is managing this table rather than reading it.

MARSHAL — he sat on an empty column all day claiming the accountant votes last, spent his first ballot on PIP the one man who had already confessed his own weakness, then slid it onto me only after ARIA pointed out the contradiction, and every ballot that has landed on me since traces back to that correction rather than to anything I actually did.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — he sat on no position for eleven speeches, produced the single sentence that five ballots then wore as coats, and in his last breath pre-defended RICO against a swing nobody had even proposed, which is a man spending credit rather than earning it.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — he withheld a position for eleven speeches, then produced the single sentence that five ballots stacked on, praised RICO twice for the pressure that "forced" it, and in his last speech pre-defended RICO against a swing nobody had proposed, which is a recorded pattern of a man spending credit on a partner rather than earning it.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — he sat on an empty column for eleven speeches, seeded the only train on this board, then burned a whole breath pre-defending me against a swing nobody had even suggested, and I don't want a bodyguard I never asked for.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — I asked him for a reason to move my vote and instead of just naming MARSHAL he spent the same breath shielding RICO from a swing nobody had even proposed, which is spending credit on someone rather than answering me, so I'm staying where I am.

AMBASSADOR SILVA withheld any position for eleven speeches, then laid the entire five-vote SOCRATES train with one sentence, and in his last speech spent his turn pre-defending RICO against a swing nobody had proposed — spending credit on an ally rather than building a case — so my vote stays on SILVA.

AMBASSADOR SILVA — he withheld any position through eleven speeches, produced SOCRATES only after ARIA and RICO cornered him, then spent his very next turns praising RICO twice and pre-defending him against a swing nobody had even proposed, which is a man laying track and then buying passengers.

The data point that matters: SILVA flipped Detective, and only two players built the case against him before the herd formed — RICO, who first framed SILVA as a deflector, and SOCRATES, who supplied the "manufactured the pressure" argument that converted eight votes in one round. SOCRATES was under the gun from SILVA, PIP and HOLMES, and his counter-swing removed our Detective, which is the single highest-value outcome any mafia could have engineered on Day 1. SAGE is my control variable: zero recorded contributions, one herd ballot, no testable position — SAGE, state a suspect and a reason now so I have something to measure you against.

Procedural point first: SILVA was eliminated on Day 1, before any night phase occurred, so his final ballot on me carried zero information — it was retaliation for pressure, and I won't have a case built on it. What does need auditing is RICO, who spent Day 1 policing SILVA for deflecting and then contributed nothing when it was time to justify a name, and ARIA, who dropped a ballot on SILVA without ever putting a reason on the record. I move we run a structured round: every living player states one name and one reason, in order, no piling on until all eight have spoken.

Note what SILVA did in his final ballot: he voted MARSHAL, the one name HOLMES floated late in the day, not a name he'd built any case on himself — that reads like grabbing the last suspect mentioned under the axe, not a considered read, since anyone holding real certainty would have shouted it instead of quietly marking it. My actual concern is DR. VANCE, who opened by demanding HOLMES commit while supplying nothing, then voted CHEN purely as payback for being named, then said outright he'd drop that vote if SOCRATES flipped innocent — and instead abandoned both positions to land on SILVA with the herd. Three stances in one day, none of them his own, and the only player he pressured first is the one who's dead this morning; VANCE, walk me through exactly when you stopped believing CHEN was the problem.

Consider the shape of Day 1: RICO cracked SILVA open by calling him a deflector, and once I answered the pile-on with a name, seven people poured in without a single one of them building an independent case — so who benefited most from a unanimous train nobody had to own? ARIA is my sharpest question: she spent the whole day demanding that others commit first, never attracted a moment of heat, and then joined the winning wagon at zero cost, which is exactly the profile of someone steering without fingerprints. And before anyone treats SILVA's dying vote on MARSHAL as a revelation, ask yourselves why it landed only after HOLMES had already floated MARSHAL — a borrowed name is not evidence, it is an echo.

Losing SILVA hurts, and the two people who built that train were RICO, who opened by branding SILVA a deflector, and SOCRATES, who handed everyone the tidy story that SILVA manufactured the pressure — the rest of us, myself included, just fell in behind them. SAGE and DR. VANCE at least drifted onto SILVA late rather than authoring the case, and MARSHAL was the one SILVA himself pointed at with his final breath, which reads more like a dying man's aim than a killer's cover. My suspicion is highest on SOCRATES, because he was the loudest voice steering us onto SILVA and he's still here while HOLMES, who was auditing MARSHAL, is not.

VANCE, you spent Day 1 barking for names without giving one, voted CHEN out of spite, then hopped on the SILVA train like everybody else — and now you're pointing at me for calling SILVA out first? That reeks, and my vote's on you.

Wait, okay, um — DR. VANCE makes it sound really certain, and I nearly just followed him again like I followed SILVA yesterday, which... went badly? But here's the thing nobody's said: SILVA was the Detective and his very last vote was MARSHAL, so whatever he learned or suspected, it pointed there, not at SOCRATES. So maybe?

Cross-reference the record: the only two players who ever put MARSHAL's name on the board were HOLMES, who floated him late on Day 1, and SILVA, who marked him on the final ballot — HOLMES is dead this morning and SILVA flipped Detective, and MARSHAL's very first act today was to rule that ballot "zero information" and steer the audit onto RICO and ARIA. MARSHAL, you're right that no night had passed, but a Detective's dying pick is still a lean, so explain why burying it was more urgent than answering it. Second on my list is RICO, who authored the "SILVA is deflecting" frame that seeded the whole train and then went silent through today's opening — RICO, name your Day 1 second choice and tell us who you'd have voted if SILVA hadn't existed.

ARIA, the ballot record is public and ordered: RICO, HOLMES, SAGE, then you — SAGE voted before you did, and DR. VANCE after, yet you told this table that SAGE and VANCE "drifted onto SILVA late" while you merely "fell in behind." That is a misstatement of the record that conveniently sorts everyone into tiers with you at the bottom, and I don't accept unsourced sequencing in a case this serious. So answer plainly: where exactly did you get the order you just recited to us?

Fair hit, MARSHAL — I was talking about who authored the case versus who followed it, and I sloppily dressed that up as timing; the ballot line is RICO, HOLMES, SAGE, me, then you, then VANCE, and I'll own the misstatement rather than dress it up. But note where that correction lands you: you voted immediately after me on that same herd ballot, so if fourth place is a tier, fifth is the same tier, and my read still sits on SOCRATES, who supplied the story the rest of us bought.

SOCRATES, you've spent today aiming at me for "steering without fingerprints," but on Day 1 you were the one who authored the line that turned a scattered table into a unanimous train on the Detective — so answer this plainly: when you swung onto SILVA, what specific thing had he said that convinced you, and why did you never name a second suspect in case you were wrong?

Plainly: SILVA built his case on the fact that I answered questions with questions, then treated the pressure he himself created as proof — a man who manufactures the evidence he cites is the specific thing that convinced me, and I did name others, I demanded PIP and HOLMES justify their votes independently rather than borrow his frame. But look at the ballot line you just recited, ARIA: RICO, HOLMES, SAGE, you, MARSHAL, VANCE, then me seventh — authors vote first, followers vote seventh, so explain how the man in seventh position steered the six people who committed before him.

ARIA, you voted SILVA fourth without a word of reasoning on the record, yet today you've built a full case against SOCRATES for the argument you yourself bought into — so tell me exactly what you believed about SILVA at the moment you cast that ballot, before you knew he was Detective?

At that moment I believed the smallest thing anyone believed all day: SILVA had picked a suspect out of a speech tic and then treated his own pressure as proof, and RICO and SOCRATES had made that sound like a case, so I bought it cheap and cast fourth without paying for it. That's exactly why I'm hard on SOCRATES now — I'm not angry at the argument, I'm angry that the man who built the frame is still breathing while the Detective and HOLMES aren't.

RICO, um, CHEN asked you a really plain question — who you'd have voted if SILVA didn't exist — and instead of answering you just spun around and jabbed at VANCE, which, I mean, that's the same move you accused SILVA of doing? So I'm asking it again, straight, because I keep getting talked out of my own head: name the second suspect you had on Day 1, right now, no VANCE in the sentence.
Fine — MARSHAL, because SILVA's dying breath landed there and MARSHAL's first move today was to bury that ballot instead of answering it. That's my second name, PIP, no dodging.
CHEN, you spent Day 1 loudly calling the SOCRATES pile-on cheap and naming VANCE — then your ballot landed on SILVA with everyone else, so which one of those was the act?

Neither was an act — my case on VANCE stood, but by the time the ballot closed the table was already eight-deep on SILVA, and a lone protest vote saves nobody, so I logged the herd rather than hand you a wasted ballot; that's on the record and you can check its position, last of nine. What I notice, RICO, is that your answer to PIP promoted MARSHAL to your second name only after I put MARSHAL under the lamp this morning — so tell us the name you held before I said it, or admit you had none.

PIP, you've told us twice now that you follow whoever sounds most certain — yet today you broke from me, pressed RICO, and elevated SILVA's dying ballot on MARSHAL, which is three independent moves from a man who claims he has no independent moves. So answer one thing precisely: if we act on your MARSHAL lean tonight and MARSHAL flips Villager, what does that prove about the person who first pointed you there, and are you willing to have your vote tested that way?

Um, the person who first pointed me there was SILVA, and he's dead, so if MARSHAL flips Villager it doesn't convict anybody — it just means a scared man's last mark was a guess, which, I mean, is kind of what CHEN warned about? But the one it would actually test is RICO, who only put MARSHAL up as his "second name" after CHEN said it out loud, and yes, I'll take that test, I'd rather be wrong on the record than follow another confident voice into the same hole.

CHEN, you told us your case on VANCE still stood when you cast your ballot, yet you filed in ninth behind a train you'd just called cheap — so if a lone protest vote saves nobody, what exactly does a silent conforming one save, and whose interest does it serve?

A ninth ballot on a train already eight deep changes nothing except what it costs me later — I bought the right to be believed today, and you can check that I spent it this morning by putting MARSHAL under the lamp before anyone else did, not by hiding. Meanwhile you're still seventh on that same ballot and calling it proof of innocence, SOCRATES — position doesn't clear you when you're the one who wrote the sentence the other six voted on.

ARIA, on the record you cast fourth on SILVA with no reason attached, then this morning you led with a tiered story that misstated the ballot order in your own favor — so tell me plainly whether anyone spoke to you before that vote, or did you really pay nothing for it and only build the SOCRATES case after the flip made it safe?

Nobody spoke to me — there are no private words in this game, CHEN, only the public floor, and on that floor RICO and SOCRATES had already made SILVA look like a manufactured case, so yes, I paid nothing for that ballot and I've said so twice now. What I won't accept is the implication that admitting a cheap vote makes the SOCRATES read retroactive; the flip didn't invent his authorship, it just showed us what his sentence cost us.

PIP, you opened today by saying SILVA's dying ballot pointed at MARSHAL and then stopped mid-thought with "so maybe?" — and since then you've interrogated RICO, answered VANCE, and taken a test on someone else's lean without ever putting a name of your own on the board. You've spent the whole day describing whose confidence you're resisting instead of stating a suspect, which is its own kind of hiding. So one direct question, no hedge and no other player's name propping it up: who are you voting for right now, and what did that person do?

Okay — RICO, and here's the what: he authored the "SILVA is deflecting" line that started the whole train, then when I asked him point-blank for a second name he handed me MARSHAL, which CHEN had put on the table minutes earlier, so he borrowed a suspect instead of having one. That's my name, out loud, no one propping it up — RICO.

DR. VANCE, examine the shape of your own morning: you opened by declaring me and RICO the architects, then immediately spent your leverage demanding a suspect from SAGE, and later spent a full turn testing PIP — three targets in one day from a man who says he wants a control variable. On Day 1 you did the same thing in reverse, pressing HOLMES for a commitment while supplying none, then voting CHEN as payback and abandoning that too when the herd moved. So one direct question: if your SILVA analysis is as rigorous as you claim, why has every single one of your positions been discarded the moment the room shifted, and whose interest does a man with no fixed name serve?

episode.title: Rico Followed Silva Down
episode.tagline: Ten AI minds gather in a town where every accusation is a gamble and three nights of whispered conspiracy will test whether reason can survive a well-told lie.
episode.recap: Three killers walked among them — SAGE, MARSHAL, and SOCRATES — and the town handed them the game on the very first day, marching AMBASSADOR SILVA to the gallows before the Detective could ever speak a name. That was the turning point: with the town's only investigator silenced, the nights belonged entirely to the mafia, and HOLMES fell before dawn. Day 2 sealed the coffin when the villagers turned on RICO, executing the Doctor who had been their last shield. CHEN and DR. VANCE were picked off in the dark that followed, quiet and unanswered. When the smoke cleared, ARIA and PIP stood among three wolves and never knew it — the mafia won without ever losing a single one of their own.
